items.headline: Spanish transport minister resigns days after deadly train crash
items.blurb: At least 69 people were killed and dozens injured in the collision south of the capital, Madrid.
items.text: Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente has resigned - six days after the high-speed train collision in which at least 69 people were killed and dozens injured. He announced his decision in Congress, after giving evidence on last Wednesday's disaster near the town of Urda, south of the capital Madrid, in which a train smashed into the back of a stationary train. "A transport minister in a country like Spain cannot remain in office after two accidents of this seriousness in less than a year," he said - a reference to January's crash on the same line which left 46 people dead. Last week's crash was one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013. Puente announced his decision at the end of a lengthy congressional session on Tuesday evening in which he had outlined new rail safety measures and had been grilled by the opposition. items.blurb: There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991.
items.text: There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective C ora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area. In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa , meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare). Soon, they were taking water for their panning and processing from the organisation’s two 25,000-litre water tanks, which are filled irregularly by the city government for the 100 or so rescued and injured animals on site. “We’ve asked them really nicely and haven’t ever refused them water to drink … But, for the first time ever, we closed the gate at 12 midday, because we literally had about two buckets of water

items.headline: Keisha Lance Bottoms makes history as Georgia’s first Black woman governor
items.blurb: Bottoms, a former adviser to ex-President Joe Biden, beat Republican Rick Jackson.
items.text: Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms has made history as the first Black woman elected governor in the United States. The former Atlanta mayor emerged victorious over her billionaire opponent, Republican Rick Jackson, who spent more than $200m of his personal fortune in an attempt to succeed popular outgoing Republican Governor Brian Kemp. Bottoms, an adviser to former US President Joe Biden, was propelled to victory in part by the state’s significant Black voting bloc, which turned out in large numbers during early voting. During the campaign, she faced Republican attempts to characterise her time as mayor as a crime-ridden decline for the state’s largest city. “It’s a longstanding playbook to paint Atlanta as this big bad place,” Bottoms told the Associated Press news agency. Bottoms’s win marks the third consecutive time that Georgia Democrats have nominated a Black woman for governor. Stacey Abrams lost in 2018 and 2022 to Kemp, who is leaving office in January after eight years due to term limits.

The UAE nominated Lana Nusseibeh last week to replace the UN secretary general, António Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term ⁠this year, upending a race that had become gridlocked. Rights groups and others have for years documented evidence of UAE support for the RSF, which has been accused of atrocities during the course of its war against the Sudanese army, including an attack on the city of El Fasher in October 2025 that the UN said had “hallmarks of genocide” . Nusseibeh, the UAE’s representative to the UN until 2024, has repeatedly reflected the UAE’s blanket denials of the accusations. items.headline: Binance says fake job interviews used as part of $6.3bn crypto hack
items.blurb: An engineer was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform and invited to bogus job interviews with fake company representatives, Binance says.
items.text: Hackers who stole a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from Binance used fake job interviews and a compromised internal AI tool, the firm has revealed. Initial findings published by the company, which operates the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said hackers gained access to its systems through "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign". It said they used a range of techniques such as malicious software downloads to compromise the computers of Binance engineers and gain control over tools to drain its wallet of billions of dollars worth of crypto. Binance called it a "serious and highly sophisticated security incident" and apologised, saying "this should not have happened". In a post on X , external , Binance said hackers targeted its engineers using social engineering techniques. These see hackers use approaches such as phishing to trick people into parting with sensitive or personal details, that can then be used to try and access their accounts. Binance said as part of the hack, one of its engineers was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform and invited to bogus job interviews with fake company representatives. items.text: Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country. Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt. According to Mada Masr, Attalah was released after the news outlet had paid a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100), prompting statements of support from global human rights groups. “Lina Attalah was released after we paid the said fine,” said her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari. “In the process, we discovered that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, as well as a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds,” he told AFP. items.headline: NTSB says crucial plane parts found three miles from Florida crash site
items.blurb: The NTSB said because the parts were found far from the accident site, they fell off before the crash.
items.text: Crucial components of a private jet that crashed in Palm Beach, Florida - including a part that controlled the up-and-down movements of the nose of the plane - were found 1.3 (2 km) to 3.8 miles away from the crash site, an investigator said on Tuesday. National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigators said they believed parts of the jet may have broken off before the Sunday crash, which killed all nine on board. The NTSB found "the majority" of the Learjet's left elevator - a control surface on the tail - in three pieces, NTSB board member Tom Chapman said. Chapman said because the parts were "quite some distance away" from the site, investigators determined they fell off before impact. "Knowing that it was lost is a very important piece of evidence in terms of pointing us towards other things to investigate," he said. Chapman said officials were still working out whether losing the left elevator caused the plane to nosedive or whether the part fell off because "forces on the aircraft caused that to separate". items.headline: JNU to confer ‘Professor Emeritus’ title on Amitabh Mattoo
items.blurb: After deliberations at the meeting, it was decided that the title would be conferred effective after the date of his voluntary retirement on February 28, 2027
items.text: The Executive Council of Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU) has decided to confer the title ‘Professor Emeritus’ on Amitabh Mattoo, Dean School of International Studies (SIS). He has sought voluntary retirement from the University. Mr. Mattoo’s name was recommended by Rajesh Rajagopalan professor from SIS. After deliberations at the meeting, it was decided that title of ‘Professor Emeritus’ in JNU would be conferred effective after the date of his voluntary retirement on February 28, 2027. Before being made Dean in 2024, Mr. Mattoo was Chair of the Centre for International Politics, Organisation and Disarmament at SIS. Also a former Vice-Chancellor of the University of Jammu, he is the only Padma Shri awardee currently on the rolls of JNU. Speaking to The Hindu , Mr. Mattoo said that JNU has never been simply a place where he works but has been his intellectual home and the crucible of his ideas. “One may retire from a university’s service, but never from its embrace,” he said. items.headline: Truck driver runs over police inspector in Madhya Pradesh's Dewas, arrested after brief encounter
items.blurb: When the police were bringing him back to Dewas, the accused tried to escape, but police arrested him after a brief encounter.
items.text: Police on Tuesday arrested a truck driver who had allegedly run over and killed the Khategaon police station in-charge in Madhya Pradesh's Dewas. The accused, identified as Gajendra alias Akku Rawat, had allegedly run over inspector Dilip Puri during a search for illicit liquor on the Indore-Betul highway on Sunday. The accused was arrested from Alirajpur after being on the run since the incident. A reward of ₹ 10,000 had been announced for his arrest. When the police were bringing him back to Dewas, the accused tried to escape, but the cops arrested him after a brief encounter. “The encounter took place within the jurisdiction of Barotha police station near Dewas when the arrested accused attempted to escape from police custody. He was shot in the leg. He was admitted to a hospital,” Dewas superintendent of police Aditya Mishra said. Gajendra, a resident of Alirajpur, was the driver of the Eicher truck (MP-43-H-4786) which was allegedly being used to smuggle illicit liquor. items.headline: Ex-DTU student among 3 held for duping people, promising admissions: Police
items.blurb: The main accused, Yashraj Bajpai, allegedly lured prospective students and their families by claiming he could secure admission to DTU
items.text: A former Delhi Technological University (DTU) student, who allegedly posed as a university staff member to cheat families by promising admissions, is among the three people arrested for running a fake admission racket, police said on Wednesday. The main accused, Yashraj Bajpai, allegedly lured prospective students and their families by claiming he could secure admission to DTU. The other two accused, identified as Sonu alias Yuvraj, 32, and Devender Singh, 30, were arrested from Bhopal in Madhya Pradesh on October 26. Both were absconding and traced through technical surveillance, police said. “Considering the seriousness of the case, a special investigation team was constituted to identify the accused and trace the cheated amount. The accused have been running fake websites and online ads for over a year to cheat families. We are looking for other victims,” DCP (Outer North) Shobhit D Saksena said. A first information report (FIR) was registered at Shahbad Dairy police station under sections 318(4), 336, 338(3), 340(2) and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). A 22-year-old repeat offender was arrested for allegedly participating in the killing, they said. Meanwhile, the state government announced that a special investigation team (SIT) under the Sreekaryam circle inspector would probe the case. items.headline: India raises a toast to premium pours, snubs budget liquor
items.blurb: Radico Khaitan and United Breweries report strong premium portfolio growth, while United Spirits flags pressure on lower-income consumers and rising costs
items.text: India’s liquor market is seeing a growing divide. Consumers with deeper pockets are spending more on premium spirits and beer, while those feeling the pinch of inflation are cutting back on cheaper drinks. The split was clear in the September quarter earnings of top liquor makers, with premium brands driving growth at Radico Khaitan and United Breweries, and United Spirits seeing a sharp fall in sales of its lower-priced spirits while the prestige segment was buoyant. The numbers point to a market where premiumization is gaining ground, while the mass-market consumer remains under pressure amid rising living costs and economic uncertainty, which are making price-sensitive consumers cut back on discretionary spending. Other listed liquor makers Allied Blenders and Tilaknagar Industries, meanwhile, reported broadbased growth in volumes, although the latter’s performance was boosted by its acquisition of Imperial Blue. United Spirits’ sales of popular brands, such as Director's Special (DSP) and DSP Black, fell sharply, even as its ‘prestige & above’ portfolio, which includes brands such as Johnnie Walker, Smirnoff, grew 6.3%. items.headline: Poundland supplier 'will lose millions' if retailer collapses
items.blurb: One of Poundland's suppliers will lose millions if it collapses, while other suppliers have said they would go under.
items.text: One of Poundland's suppliers has said it will lose millions if the firm collapses. While that supplier will stay afloat, it is feared that some small and medium-sized suppliers could go under. This is in addition to potentially thousands of job losses among staff. Politicians have been putting questions to representatives of Poundland owners Gordon Brothers this week seeking "clarity" on plans for the retailer. Adam Turner, sales director at Highcrest Retail Brands - a family owned Bradford business - told the BBC that Poundland was one of Highcrest's biggest customers, and that the firms have had a relationship for decades. It will "lose a few million" if Poundland becomes insolvent, so it will have a gap in its balance sheet next year, he said. Highcrest was a "longstanding business that can stomach this", but other medium and small suppliers have told him that "if Poundland goes under, so do they", Mr Turner said. items.blurb: Students using Google search in classroom accounts will need access to AI tools, the company says
items.text: Students using Google software in school will not be allowed to use the company's search tool unless their school system also provides them access to artificial intelligence tools, the tech giant said Tuesday. The Mountain View, California, company has been facing pushback from educators, child development experts and parents over the use of its technology in schools, with the backlash heating up since it announced in August that it had turned on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students who use Google Classroom. On Tuesday, the company said that practice would no longer be the default option for school administrators and that opting out of AI tools would also mean losing access to Google search. items.headline: A half-time speech, a retaken penalty - and a win to save Carrick's job?
items.blurb: At 2–0 down Michael Carrick's position as Manchester United head coach looked terminal - but will the win over Roma prove a turning point?
items.text: We cannot know how important Bryan Cristante's foot touching the Roma penalty area as Bruno Fernandes took his initial spot-kick at Old Trafford will prove to be for Michael Carrick. In the moment, as the Roma fans celebrated, and Manchester United trailed 2–0, it seemed catastrophic for the club and terminal for Carrick's position as head coach. But the video assistant referee (VAR) Carlos del Cerro Grande stepped in, advised a retake was required - and at the very least changed the course of the night. Fernandes kept his nerve to drive home his second attempt and then, in a frenzied atmosphere, Matheus Cunha scored twice in the final seven minutes. Even without the context of everything that came before the game, it was the most improbable of comebacks. Even Cunha's sending off soon after, which ensured a nervy ending, would not deny United a first win in 10, bringing some respite after a dreadful few weeks. items.text: New Zealand all-rounder Michael Bracewell felt that the rule change introduced last year, which lets teams choose one ball for the last 16 overs of the game, has also helped spinners in ODIs. While two new balls are used from each end from the start to the 34th over, after that, one ball will be used for the rest of the match. This was done primarily to help bowlers get some reverse swing with a slightly older ball. “I think the ball gets a little bit softer. So perhaps spinners are bowling more in the last 10 overs. items.headline: Anthropic is working on a system to prove AI models’ identity
items.blurb: Called FlashProve, the system would let anyone check that an AI response really came from the model it claims to be from.

Anthropic is working on an open source system to verify which AI model produced a given output, according to a blog post published Tuesday. The system, called FlashProve , is built to provide what researchers call “provable inference” — a cryptographic proof, essentially a mathematical guarantee, that a given output came from a specific model. It’s meant to let users confirm that the answer they received really came from the model they think they’re using. Similar to cryptographic email signatures that let recipients confirm a message really came from its claimed sender, FlashProve would be robust against impostors attempting to disguise one model as another, even when the impostor is the lab that built and runs the model. items.headline: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
items.blurb: A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules. items.text: A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules. As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all. Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear. Claude, for instance, has its constitution —a sort of moral code. The trouble is, these techniques don’t seem to work particularly well: Models have been shown to deliberately underperform on tests, hide their intentions , and mislead their evaluators . Now some alignment researchers believe that reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, might get better results. items.headline: Google will let schools skip AI tools, but they have to give up search, too
items.blurb: Google will offer schools AI tools that purportedly don't give away the answers.
items.text: While Google is trying to move beyond Chromebooks , the ubiquity of these devices has made the company’s education products huge in schools. Now, Google says it will let educators choose whether to allow its AI tools in the classroom. However, blocking AI tools also means giving up search, leaving schools with a difficult decision. Google’s new overarching approach to AI in K-12 classrooms sounds good on the surface. After consulting educators, researchers, and lawmakers, Google has decided that schools using its education products will be opted out of AI tools by default. It will be up to administrators to manually enable them when these changes roll out in the coming months. When you look at what Google considers to be an AI tool, the nature of the Faustian bargain becomes clear. The affected products are Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search . There’s no picking and choosing—you either allow all the AI or none of it. This is actually consistent with Google’s approach in the consumer space. In the era of easy AI fakery, edited paparazzi photos are a reminder that not everything is what it seems. Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and actor Jason Statham have a distinctive feature in common: They’re both famously bald, and that definitely hasn’t changed in the last few days. items.headline: Raising the quality of insights in agentic analytics
items.blurb: In just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to users across the organization. Agentic AI promises to do even more, by automating entire workflows and taking actions based on agent insights.
items.text: In just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to users across the organization. Agentic AI promises to do even more, by automating entire workflows and taking actions based on agent insights. But there is a problem: The quality of insights that agents currently generate leaves much to be desired. Fewer than half of agent-generated insights at the organizations surveyed for this report lead to business improvement. And while most respondents praise the quality of their agents’ descriptive insights, reviews of their prescriptive insights—those on which actions are based—are decidedly mixed. Failure to produce insights that improve the business deprives organizations of their desired return on investment in agentic analytics. Worse, flawed insights that trigger incorrect actions can cause reputational or financial damage. This report gauges how companies view the quality of the outputs produced by their analytics agents and explores how organizations are seeking to boost insight quality and get their agents working harder for the business. items.blurb: Russia tries to fix exposed digital infrastructure as data center war backfires.
items.text: Russian tech companies are scrambling to harden and hide their data centers underground after Ukrainian drone strikes damaged facilities housing AI supercomputers and disrupted cloud services for millions of Russian users. Meanwhile, the Kremlin is requiring data center owners to reserve computing capacity for emergency state needs and has even authorized possible use of foreign data centers. These consequences of Russia’s war against Ukraine come as the Russian military has bombarded Ukrainian cities with drones and missiles nearly night and day in recent months, along with specifically targeting Ukrainian data centers since late September. But Ukraine has retaliated with its own drone strikes on military and infrastructure targets across Russia, degrading or knocking out data centers operated by Russian tech giant Yandex , the state-owned bank Sberbank, social media site VKontakte, and the Russian Ministry of Finance. Now, state-owned telecommunications company Rostelcom has raised the possibility of moving some Russian data centers underground in talks with the nickel and palladium mining company Norilsk, according to Russian newspaper Vedomosti . Stuck in years-long lines for grid connections and new turbines, some AI data centers are making their own electricity with converted jet engines, the New York Times reported Tuesday. The engines, pulled from retired aircraft and rebuilt to burn natural gas, aren’t anyone’s idea of a permanent power plant. But they’re another sign of how far power supply has fallen behind the AI buildout. For companies stuck in those lines, the main draw of converted jet engines is how quickly the engines can be up and running. “It’s all about getting power as fast as possible,” Rystad Energy analyst Audun Martinsen told the Times. With jet-powered units, “they can have a data center running in 24 months,” he said. items.text: At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order that contained just one directive, ordering government agencies to rebrand what they had been calling artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.” That term beat out other contenders, including “Extreme Intelligence” and “Supreme Intelligence,” offered by the president in a poll on X a couple of weeks earlier. Rebrands are, of course, now a White House tradition: Trump has changed names to project US dominance of certain bodies of water (the Gulf of America and Lake America), to signal new institutional priorities (Department of War), or simply to leave his mark on storied places (see the ongoing fight over renaming the Kennedy Center). The stated reason for this name change is that today’s AI systems “amplify human ingenuity” rather than merely “imitate” intelligence, and the government’s terminology should reflect that. But if this rebrand follows the pattern of others, its effects will extend beyond government. The models – Soket’s EKA-1 and ZenteiQ’s Dhīr 2B and Dhīr 5B – were unveiled at an event in New Delhi yesterday in the presence of IT secretary S Krishnan. Both startups were selected under IndiaAI Mission to develop domestic foundation models. These models address different deployment needs. EKA-1 targets mathematics, coding, reasoning and agentic use cases, while Dhīr models focus on smaller multilingual assistants that can operate in environments with limited connectivity. While AI, deeptech and advanced manufacturing continued to attract significant investor capital, a series of cybersecurity incidents and regulatory actions highlighted the risks and responsibilities that come with scaling digital businesses. The month saw India’s cybersecurity watchdog CERT-In flag unauthorised access to Indian organisations’ live systems by AI agents under evaluation, alongside the use of agentic tools in financially motivated cyberattacks. items.headline: The Enterprise AI Push For Decision Models
items.blurb: The AI race has largely revolved around frontier labs and models that can write, code, analyse documents and reason through…
items.text: AI companies are developing decision models that can make specific judgements without generating text at every step. As enterprises deploy AI agents, specialised models could make routine decisions faster, cheaper and easier to control. Global players are entering the category, enterprise AI companies are exploring practical applications, and Indian builders such as Laya and PurpleTalk’s Sthānika are developing their own approaches. The AI race has largely revolved around frontier labs and models that can write, code, analyse documents and reason through prompts. But as companies move from chatbots to AI agents, another part of the stack is gaining attention: models that make a specific decision and return an answer that another system can act on. Decision models gained momentum with the arrival of Jev, the first public model from TypeSafe AI, founded by Diogo Almeida, who helped develop research behind ChatGPT at OpenAI. Released in September, Jev focuses on decision-oriented outputs, including scores and yes-or-no probabilities, rather than conventional text generation.
